land.text: 'After the last count died in 1497, Armagnac was united temporarily with the crown'

successors.note: The page says 'temporarily'; Cliopatria's last shape is 1496.

capitals.name: Lectoure
capitals.note: The page says Lectoure 'lost capital status to Auch in the mid-17th century'; its infobox gives Auch as capital (the later one).

keyframe_review.note: 7,079 km2: the Gers (Gers 20/24 gazetteer cells, with edge cells of Hautes-Pyrénées, Landes, Pyrénées-Atlantiques and Tarn-et-Garonne). The infobox has no area. The page: 'County created: before 960' (infobox); the elder branch failed in 1245 and Géraud V of Fezensaguet was 'confirmed as comte d'Armagnac in 1256; however, at his death (1285) the two counties were separated anew' (footnote 3). Cliopatria draws no change at 1256 or 1285.
Unverified: page budget. 6,961 km2, a 1.7% outline revision no page dates (Géraud V's union with Fezensaguet is 1256, its end 1285).
Unverified: page budget. 6,985 km2, outline revision; the 1285 separation of the two counties (Armagnac page, footnote 3) is not visible in the shape.
Unverified: page budget. 6,844 km2, the shape that holds after the 1285 separation; no page dates the outline change.

correction.text: the shape unchanged, years 1333-1360 (ceded to England in 1360)

keyframe_review.note: Years 1333-1360 only. 'the southern part of France, including Armagnac, was ceded to England by the Treaty of Brétigny (1360)'; the Brétigny page has it drafted on 8 May 1360 and ratified on 24 October 1360 and does not list Armagnac by name. Cliopatria keeps the shape to 1362 and has no shape 1363-1374.

correction.text: the county of Armagnac as before 1360, back under the French king from 1369

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1369-1374 for years Cliopatria lacks: 'the count of Armagnac appealed to the French king for help in 1369' because the Black Prince's rule had become harsh; by submitting to Charles V noble families like the Armagnacs kept much of their power (paraphrase). HYW page: 'before the end of 1369 all of Aquitaine was in full revolt.' The county is again the 1333 shape; 1361-1368 it is English (no shape).

23,633 km2 = the Gers plus Aveyron 29/36 (the county of Rodez), Lot 16/21, Tarn-et-Garonne 14/18 (Lomagne and Auvillars) and 5 cells of Saône-et-Loire (Charolais). The page: Jean I and his successors 'joined to Armagnac the comté of Rodez and that of Carlat, and the vicomtés of Lomagne and Auvillars, Comminges and briefly Charolais', undated; Carlat (Cantal) is not in the shape, Lot (Quercy) is not on the page. The infobox has no area; the shape is 3.4 times the 1333 shape because of these acquisitions. Kept: unverified in outline.

correction.text: the 1385 shape plus Charolais for 1385-1389 (from 1390 as drawn)

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria drops Charolais in 1385, but the Armagnac page says Jean III alienated it in 1390 and this page that 'Count Bernard VII of Armagnac sold the county to Duke Philip II of Burgundy in 1390' (Bernard VII succeeded Jean III only in 1391, Bernard VII page). Corrected: the 1385 shape plus Charolais through 1389. The shape also drops Lot and most of Tarn-et-Garonne and gains 10/20 of Hautes-Pyrénées (Bigorre), changes no page opened explains (the county-of-foix dossier dates the sale of Bigorre to John I of Foix in 1407).

Bernard VII 'also became Count of Comminges in 1412' after prolonged fighting; Cliopatria's shape lacks Comminges (Haute-Garonne) and has lost the Bigorre cells in 1407. Corrected: the 1407 shape plus Comminges for 1412-1418 (Bernard VII died on 12 June 1418; the page does not say what became of Comminges). 1407-1411 and 1419-1421 as drawn.

Unverified in outline: 13,774 km2, Gers and Aveyron (Rodez) as in 1407. Bernard VII's infobox titles 'Count of Armagnac 1391–1418', 'Count of Fézensac', 'Count of Rodez', 'Count of Pardiac' fit the Gers and Aveyron cells; the page does not say what became of Rodez, Fézensac or Pardiac after 1418.

Unverified in outline: 14,009 km2. The Armagnac infobox lists 'King Henry VI of England 1422–1453' and then 'King Charles VII of France 1453–1461' among its rulers; the HYW page: 'the English were decisively defeated at the Battle of Castillon on 17 July 1453.' The shape is unchanged in area and no page opened says the county itself passed to England in 1422. Count Jean V 'opposed King Louis XI' and was killed at Lectoure in 1473: see the ledger (no shape change is drawn).
Same polygon as 1453. The last count died in 1497 (page); Cliopatria's shape ends in 1496, so a one-year keyframe 1497 follows.
New one-year keyframe: 'After the last count died in 1497, Armagnac was united temporarily with the crown.' The 1492 polygon holds through 1497, the dossier's last year.

region.text: the county of Armagnac around Lectoure and Auch (the Gers)

ledger.note: 1206: the County of Armagnac, in Gascony, is the earliest year of Cliopatria's shape. The page dates its creation earlier ('County created: before 960', infobox; the title was established in 960), so 1206 only starts the drawing.

1256: Géraud V of Fezensaguet is confirmed as Count of Armagnac, rejoining the lines after the elder branch failed in 1245; 'at his death (1285) the two counties were separated anew' (footnote 3). Cliopatria draws no change.

region.text: Armagnac, in the southern part of France ceded to England

ledger.note: 1360: Armagnac is ceded to England by the Treaty of Brétigny. 'the southern part of France, including Armagnac, was ceded to England by the Treaty of Brétigny (1360)'. Brétigny page: drafted 8 May and ratified 24 October 1360 at Calais, without naming Armagnac.

region.text: Armagnac, back under the French crown

ledger.note: 1369: the count appeals to the French king and Armagnac returns to French allegiance. 'the count of Armagnac appealed to the French king for help in 1369'; by submitting to Charles V the Armagnacs kept much of their power (paraphrase). The page does not say when the English lost control; Cliopatria shows the county again from 1375.

1375: Cliopatria's shape grows to include the county of Rodez. 'Jean I, comte d'Armagnac (1319–1373) and his successors joined to Armagnac the comté of Rodez and that of Carlat'; the page gives no year, so the date is Cliopatria's.

region.text: the vicomtés of Lomagne and Auvillars (Tarn-et-Garonne)

ledger.note: 1375: the viscounties of Lomagne and Auvillars join, in Cliopatria's shape ('the vicomtés of Lomagne and Auvillars', undated on the page).

region.text: the Lot, in Cliopatria's 1375 shape only

ledger.note: 1375: Cliopatria's shape also holds the Lot (Quercy), which no page opened gives to Armagnac.

region.text: Charolais, held briefly by the counts

ledger.note: 1375: Charolais joins, in Cliopatria's shape. The Charolais page: 'In 1314 it passed to Robert's second son John, whose daughter Beatrice married Count John I of Armagnac in 1327'; the Armagnac page lists Charolais, 'briefly', among the acquisitions. Neither dates the arrival.

region.text: Lot and most of Tarn-et-Garonne, leaving the 1385 shape

ledger.note: 1385: Cliopatria's shape loses Lot and most of Tarn-et-Garonne (Quercy and Lomagne). No page opened explains this.

region.text: the Hautes-Pyrénées cells (Bigorre) entering the 1385 shape

ledger.note: 1385: Cliopatria's shape gains Hautes-Pyrénées cells (Bigorre), for which no page opened gives a date or a counterpart.

region.text: Charolais, sold to Philip II of Burgundy

ledger.note: 1390: Charolais is sold to Burgundy. 'John's grandson Count Bernard VII of Armagnac sold the county to Duke Philip II of Burgundy in 1390' (this page); the Armagnac page: 'which Jean III alienated in 1390'. Bernard VII succeeded his brother John III in 1391 (Bernard VII page), so the pages disagree on the seller.

region.text: the Hautes-Pyrénées cells (Bigorre) leaving the shape

ledger.note: 1407: the Hautes-Pyrénées cells leave Cliopatria's shape. No page opened dates it; the county-of-foix dossier (not a page opened here) has John I of Foix buying Bigorre from Bernard VII in 1407.
1412: Bernard VII becomes Count of Comminges. 'After prolonged fighting, he also became Count of Comminges in 1412.'

1418: Bernard VII is killed ('On 12 June 1418, he was one of the first victims of the massacres') and Comminges leaves Armagnac, a bridge: the page does not say what became of Comminges; Cliopatria's 1422 shape lacks it.
1473: Louis XI's soldiers besiege Lectoure. Count Jean V 'was finally killed by the king's soldiers in 1473, in Lectoure under siege'.

1473: Louis XI controls the county and creates the Seneschalcy of Armagnac: 'In 1473, following the control of the county by Louis XI, the Seneschalcy of Armagnac was created.' The page names a last count who died in 1497, so the line did not end here.

region.text: the county of Armagnac, united with the crown

ledger.note: 1497: the last count dies and Armagnac is united with the crown. 'After the last count died in 1497, Armagnac was united temporarily with the crown.'

wars.name: Hundred Years' War

zones.text: Armagnac, in the south ceded to England in 1360

wars.outcome: Armagnac was ceded to England in 1360, the count appealed to Charles V in 1369 and the French reconquest followed ('By 1378, under King Charles V the Wise' most ceded lands were retaken); the war ended at Castillon on 17 July 1453.
wars.note: Start year 1355 is the Black Prince's devastation 'between Bordeaux and Languedoc' (Armagnac page), not the war's start; the HYW page was read for 1369, 1378 and 1453.

wars.name: Armagnac–Burgundian Civil War
wars.outcome: 'The two factions engaged in a bloody civil war that ended in 1435' (Armagnac page); Bernard VII, the Armagnac leader, was killed in the Burgundian massacre of Paris on 12 June 1418; the Treaty of Arras (1435) ended it. No Armagnac border moved.
wars.note: The pages give no start date; 1407 is the assassination of Louis of Orléans after which 'Armagnac remained attached to the cause of Orléans' (Bernard VII page).

wars.name: Siege of Lectoure
wars.outcome: Jean V was killed by the king's soldiers in Lectoure under siege in 1473 and Louis XI controlled the county; the Seneschalcy of Armagnac was created. The count line ended only in 1497.

certainty.note: No treaty line or survey on the pages opened; the Brétigny cession of 1360 names regions, not lines. The 1375-1384 acquisitions (Rodez, Lomagne, Charolais) are the softest.

notes:
Cliopatria reading by gazetteer cells: 1206-1362 is the Gers (about 7,000 km2, the Armagnac proper); 1375-1384 adds Aveyron (Rodez), Lot, Tarn-et-Garonne (Lomagne, Auvillars) and Charolais (Saône-et-Loire); 1385-1406 drops Lot, most of Tarn-et-Garonne and Charolais and adds the Hautes-Pyrénées (Bigorre); 1407 drops Bigorre; 1422-1496 is the Gers plus Aveyron. No shape 1363-1374.
Corrected: the Brétigny cession (loss 1360, back 1369, new keyframe 1369-1374); Charolais kept to 1390; Comminges 1412-1418 (the 1418 end is a bridge, confidence 1); the 1497 end (page) against Cliopatria's 1496.
Disagreements between pages: who alienated Charolais in 1390 (Jean III on the Armagnac page, Bernard VII on the Charolais page; Bernard VII succeeded in 1391); the Armagnac page's own dates for the county's creation (601 in the lead, 960, 'before 960'). The Armagnac page lists Carlat (Cantal) and Comminges among Jean I's and his successors' acquisitions without dates; Carlat is not in any shape.
Not settled (counterparts without a dossier): County of Rodez / Rouergue (county-of-rouergue ends 1065 in Cliopatria), Lomagne and Auvillars, Charolais, Comminges, Fezensaguet, and the unexplained Lot and Bigorre changes of 1375, 1385 and 1407. The 1285 separation from Fezensaguet and the 1245 failure of the elder line are on the page but draw no border.
